To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the stiffness of a continuum robot can be accurately approximated by an analytical model, and that this model can be used to design a stiffness controller that achieves a desired tip stiffness.
we developed a stiffness control method for continuum robots based on deflection sensing and we experimentally demonstrated that it works.

we introduce a stiffness controller for continuum manipulators that is based on an approximate model, uses deflection sensing to measure and control stiffness, and can be implemented by modification to existing position controllers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of continuum manipulators that are capable of performing minimally invasive surgery.
the design, analysis, and control of continuum robots, with the ultimate goal of enabling these devices to be used in minimally-invasive medical procedures.
the control of continuum robots, and more particularly, the development of a stiffness controller for surgical continuum robots.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the stiffness controller presented here enables the design of a continuum robot that can be controlled to achieve a desired stiffness at the tip, and thus can be used for a wide range of surgical applications.
the proposed stiffness control method provides a practical approach to stiffness control that can be implemented on continuum robots with existing position control systems and deflection sensing.
this work introduces the first stiffness control law for continuum robots, enabling the first experimental demonstration of stiffness control for continuum robots.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the controller can be used to achieve a desired stiffness in the continuum robot.
we have demonstrated that continuum robots are capable of stiffness control.

we developed the first continuum robot stiffness controller, which can be used in the context of continuum robots with deflection sensing, and which can be easily integrated with any existing continuum robot position controller.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the stiffness controller enables continuum robots to be operated in a manner that is more similar to conventional laparoscopic tools, which are typically used in minimally invasive surgery.

continuum robot deflection sensing can be used to achieve stiffness control, which is a significant advantage over other continuum robots that do not use deflection sensing and therefore require a separate force/torque sensor to achieve stiffness control.
continuum robots are inherently capable of stiffness control, and that the control of continuum robots is not fundamentally limited to position and force control.
